subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent bleeding into his knees and ankles and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. His maternal uncle had similar problems. Laboratory studies show an isolated prolonged PTT with a normal PT, platelet count, and bleeding time.
question: Which factor is deficient, and what is the inheritance pattern in this patient?

options.text: Factor IX deficiency; autosomal recessive
Factor XI deficiency; autosomal recessive
Factor VIII deficiency; X-linked recessive
Factor VIII deficiency; autosomal dominant
Factor XIII deficiency; X-linked recessive

explanation_correct: Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency with X-linked recessive inheritance, remembered as hemophilia Ate (eight). It produces a prolonged PTT from an intrinsic pathway defect with a normal PT and platelet studies. Clinical features include hemarthroses, especially of the knee, easy bruising, and bleeding after trauma or dental procedures; treatment includes desmopressin, factor VIII concentrate, and emicizumab.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B, which is X-linked recessive rather than autosomal recessive.
explanation_incorrect.B: Factor XI deficiency is hemophilia C, an autosomal recessive and usually milder form that is not the classic X-linked picture described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Factor VIII deficiency is X-linked recessive, not autosomal dominant; the maternal uncle history supports X-linked inheritance.
explanation_incorrect.E: Factor XIII deficiency is autosomal recessive and impairs clot stabilization rather than causing the classic hemophilia A intrinsic pathway defect.

educationalObjective: Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive factor VIII deficiency causing a prolonged PTT, hemarthroses, and bleeding after trauma or dental work.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 10-year-old boy with a bleeding history through his mother's family line presents with a hemarthrosis and excessive bleeding after a tonsillectomy. Laboratory studies show an isolated prolonged PTT. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the gene encoding factor IX.
question: Which of the following is the correct classification and treatment for this patient?

options.text: Hemophilia B, factor IX deficiency with X-linked recessive inheritance, treated with factor IX concentrate
Hemophilia A, factor VIII deficiency, treated with emicizumab
Hemophilia C, factor XI deficiency with autosomal recessive inheritance, treated with factor XI concentrate
von Willebrand disease, treated with desmopressin
Vitamin K deficiency, treated with vitamin K replacement

explanation_correct: Hemophilia B is deficiency of factor IX with X-linked recessive inheritance. Like hemophilia A, it produces a prolonged PTT and the same bleeding phenotype of hemarthroses, easy bruising, and bleeding after trauma or surgery. Treatment is factor IX concentrate; factor VIII concentrate and emicizumab are used for hemophilia A.

explanation_incorrect.B: Factor VIII deficiency is hemophilia A, not B; emicizumab is a factor VIII-mimizing therapy used in hemophilia A.
explanation_incorrect.C: Factor XI deficiency is hemophilia C with autosomal recessive inheritance; this patient has a factor IX mutation and an X-linked family history.
explanation_incorrect.D: von Willebrand disease involves defective vWF with impaired platelet adhesion, often with a prolonged bleeding time, not an isolated factor IX deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vitamin K deficiency reduces factors II, VII, IX, and X with prolongation of both PT and PTT, not an isolated factor IX defect.

educationalObjective: Hemophilia B is X-linked recessive factor IX deficiency with a prolonged PTT and is treated with factor IX concentrate.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 22-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry has a lifelong history of easy bruising and menorrhagia but no spontaneous hemarthroses. She had prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Laboratory studies show an isolated prolonged PTT, and genetic testing confirms an autosomal recessive deficiency of factor XI.
question: Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

options.text: It is X-linked recessive and predominantly affects males
It is due to factor VIII deficiency and is treated with emicizumab
It is due to factor IX deficiency with X-linked inheritance
It is autosomal recessive factor XI deficiency, treated with factor XI concentrate
It is caused by an acquired anti-factor VIII inhibitor

explanation_correct: Hemophilia C is deficiency of factor XI with autosomal recessive inheritance and a prolonged PTT. It is typically milder than hemophilia A or B and is more common in Ashkenazi Jews. Treatment is factor XI concentrate; desmopressin, factor VIII concentrate, and emicizumab are used for hemophilia A, and factor IX concentrate for hemophilia B.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hemophilia C is autosomal recessive, whereas it is hemophilias A and B that are X-linked recessive and predominantly affect males.
explanation_incorrect.B: Factor VIII deficiency is hemophilia A; emicizumab mimics factor VIII activity and is not the treatment for factor XI deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.C: Factor IX deficiency is hemophilia B with X-linked inheritance, not the autosomal recessive factor XI deficiency confirmed here.
explanation_incorrect.E: An acquired anti-factor VIII inhibitor causes an acquired coagulopathy that fails to correct on mixing; this is a congenital factor XI deficiency.

educationalObjective: Hemophilia C is autosomal recessive factor XI deficiency with a prolonged PTT, a milder bleeding tendency, and treatment with factor XI concentrate.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 9-year-old boy with hemophilia A has had several episodes of bleeding into his knees and prolonged bleeding after minor trauma. His hematology team is selecting a targeted prophylactic agent that does not require factor VIII replacement.
question: Which of the following is an appropriate targeted therapy for his specific condition?

options.text: Factor IX concentrate
Emicizumab, along with desmopressin or factor VIII concentrate
Factor XI concentrate
Deferasirox
Fresh frozen plasma as first-line routine prophylaxis

explanation_correct: Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency treated with desmopressin, factor VIII concentrate, and emicizumab. Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody that bridges factor IXa and factor X to mimic factor VIII activity, useful for prophylaxis without factor VIII replacement. The classic manifestations are hemarthroses, easy bruising, and bleeding after trauma or dental procedures.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factor IX concentrate is the treatment for hemophilia B, not factor VIII-deficient hemophilia A.
explanation_incorrect.C: Factor XI concentrate is used for hemophilia C, an autosomal recessive factor XI deficiency.
explanation_incorrect.D: Deferasirox is an iron chelator used for iron overload, not for replacing or mimicking factor VIII activity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fresh frozen plasma is not the preferred specific prophylactic therapy; factor concentrates or emicizumab are used for targeted treatment.

educationalObjective: Hemophilia A is treated with desmopressin, factor VIII concentrate, or emicizumab, which mimics factor VIII function.
